chunks: "I'd start with the requirements: how many bits, what output range, how fast it updates, how accurate it has to be, what it drives, and what supply I have.
Say I need an 8-bit, 0 to 3. 3 volts output updating at 100 kS/s for a bias or control signal. At 8 bits and 12.
9 millivolts per step, the options are: an R-2R ladder from eight GPIO pins with an op-amp buffer, a PWM output with a filter, or a DAC chip. For this, I'd use the R-2R.
Resistor tolerance sets the linearity: from a quick Monte Carlo, 8 bits with 1% resistors can be non-monotonic and have up to 2 LSB of DNL, while 0.
1% resistors keep DNL under about 0. 2 LSB, so I'd use a 0. 1% resistor network. R is 10 kilohms, so the ladder settles in well under a microsecond.
I'd add a rail-to-rail op-amp as a unity-gain buffer with offset under half an LSB, 6 millivolts, because the ladder has 10 kilohms output resistance.
The GPIO high level is the reference, so I'd either accept ratiometric accuracy or drive the ladder from buffered logic on a clean reference.
If I had a spare timer and no pins, I'd go PWM: 8 bits at 16 megahertz gives 62.
5 kilohertz, and a two-stage RC at about 47 microseconds per stage keeps ripple to about half an LSB and settles in under a millisecond. For 12 bits I'd buy a DAC chip.
Then I'd verify by sweeping all codes, checking monotonicity and step size with a good meter, and measuring settling and glitch on a scope."
